classes: A confidence interval gives a plausible range for the true value, not a single guess.
A histogram groups values into bins and shows how many fall in each bin.
A moving average smooths noise by averaging a sliding window of recent values.
A percentage is a part per hundred; always name the base it is a percentage of.
A pivot table regroups rows by categories and summarizes values per group.
A simple forecast extends the recent trend and states its uncertainty honestly.
A/B testing compares two variants on real users and judges the difference statistically.
Add all values, divide by how many there are, and report the count beside the average.
Bars compare categories, lines show change over time, and scatter plots show relationships.
Check formulas cell by cell, trace precedents, and test totals against raw sums.
Cleaning: fix formats, remove duplicates, flag missing values, and document every change.
Cohort analysis groups users by start time and tracks each group separately.
Compare centers, spreads, and sample sizes; a difference matters only beyond natural variation.
Compare early and late averages, check direction, and note any single month that breaks the pattern.
Compare totals, averages, and the change in percentage, then look for the cause.
Compound growth applies each period's growth to the new total, not the original.
Correlation means values move together; causation needs a mechanism and controlled evidence.
Count blanks per column, check patterns in what is missing, and decide fill or drop rules.
Dataset summary: count, center, spread, extremes, and the one pattern that matters.
Experiment summary: groups, sample sizes, effect size, and whether it clears significance.
Growth rate is change divided by the starting value, expressed as a percentage.
Honest charts show full axes, label sources, and never hide inconvenient points.
KPIs are the few numbers tied directly to a goal, reviewed on a fixed cadence.
Larger samples give steadier estimates; tiny samples swing wildly with one new value.
Mean is the average, median is the middle value, and mode is the most frequent value.
Misleading charts truncate axes, cherry-pick ranges, or hide sample sizes.
Multiply each value by its weight, sum the products, and divide by total weight.
Normalization rescales values to a common range so different units can be compared.
Outliers are values far from the rest; verify them before deciding whether they are errors or signals.
Percentage change is new minus old, divided by old, times one hundred.
Quality checks cover completeness, consistency, valid ranges, and duplicate records.
Quartiles split sorted data into four equal parts, showing where the middle half lies.
Range is maximum minus minimum; it shows total spread in one number.
Readable tables align numbers, label units, sort meaningfully, and highlight key rows.
Regression fits a line or curve that best predicts one value from others.
Sampling picks a subset to represent the whole; random sampling reduces selection bias.
Seasonality repeats on a calendar cycle; compare matching seasons across years.
Share of total is each part divided by the sum, shown as a percentage.
Significance asks whether a difference is larger than chance alone would plausibly produce.
Skew means one tail is longer; the mean gets pulled toward the long tail.
Standard deviation measures typical distance from the mean; larger means more spread.
Survey summary: response count, top answers with percentages, and who was surveyed.
The mode is the most common value; report how often it appears beside it.
Time series data is ordered by time; look for trend, seasonality, and sudden shifts.
Use the median when outliers skew the mean, such as incomes or house prices.
Variance is the average squared distance from the mean; its square root is standard deviation.
Weekly patterns repeat by weekday; compare same weekdays across weeks before judging.
Weight averages by their counts before combining, or the small group distorts the result.
